description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

Bibrad Disc have thoughtfully designed features to make it the easiest menstrual disc to insert, remove, and clean. Set include 1 disc 1 cotton bag 2 instruction booklet English and Spanish.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
What is the difference between menstrual cups and menstrual discs?
The cups are placed in the vaginal canal, while the discs are placed higher up in the vaginal fornix, just below the cervix. The cups are held in place by suction against the walls of the vaginal canal, while the discs are held in place by the vaginal musculature and by being placed behind the pubic bone. Cups traditionally have a stem that sits at the opening of the vaginal canal, while discs have no part that sits near the opening of the vaginal canal, making them more comfortable.

How long can I wear it?
You can wear a menstrual disc for up to 12 hours.

Are there any limits to what I can do while wearing a menstrual disc?
No! You can play sports, sleep, have sex, go to work, lounge on the couch... whatever you want. It gives you the freedom to live your best life.

Why is the menstrual disc ideal for heavy flow as well as light flow?
Menstrual discs collect your flow rather than absorbing it. Because of this, regardless of the amount of flow, the disc is great.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS -

What is the difference between a menstrual cup and a menstrual disc?
Cups sit in the vaginal canal while a disc sits further up in the vaginal fornix right under the cervix. Cups stay in place using suction against the walls of the vaginal canal. Discs, however, stay in place thanks to strong vaginal muscles and being tucked behind the pubic bone. Cups traditionally have a stem that sits in the opening of the vaginal canal whereas a disc does not have any portion that sits near the opening of the vaginal canal, making them more comfortable.


How long can I leave it in?
You can wear a menstrual disc for up to 12 hours.

Are there any limits to what I can do while wearing a menstrual disc?
No! You can exercise, swim, sleep, have sex, run, go to work, lounge on your couch--whatever you want. It gives you the freedom to live your best life.

Is it true that I can have mess-free period sex with it in?
Yes! Menstrual discs sit right under your cervix in the vaginal fornix and don’t take up any space in the vaginal canal. That leaves plenty of room for penetration.

How is the disc great for a heavy flow and also great for a light flow?
Menstrual discs collect your flow rather than absorbing it. Because of this, regardless of the amount of flow, the disc is great.

Why should I buy a set of two sizes? Which one will fit me?
Throughout your cycle, the height of your cervix can change from high to low to anywhere in between. Cervix height impacts the fit of a menstrual disc. By purchasing a set of two sizes, you can feel confident that one of the two sizes will fit at any point during your cycle.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

  2. Place your index finger and thumb into your vagina. Pull the stem of the cup gently until you can reach the base.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
A Better Way To Manage Your Period
On average, a woman will experience 30 or so years of menstruation in her lifetime, from her first period to menopause. Just one year's supply of disposable pads and tampons can cost between $60 and $120. Doing the math (and lowballing it), that's around $3,600 in a lifetime on a NECCESITY. Enter Reusable Menstrual Cups, an alternative that is equally as effective as sanitary pads and tampons.

Available in two colours, black and yellow and two sizes, 25ml and 35ml

What Size Should I Choose?

  • 25ml- For normal to light flow or those under the age of 30 who have never given birth
  • 35ml- For heavier menstruating days and everyone else

How Do I Wear One?

  1. Wash your hands thoroughly.
  2. Get into a comfortable position and fold cup to desired shape.
  3. Insert & push cup into vagina.
  4. Turn it around until cup pops back to original shape.
Note: You shouldn’t feel your menstrual cup if you’ve inserted the cup correctly. You should also be able to move, jump, sit, stand, and do other everyday activities without your cup falling out.

How Do I Take It Out?

  1. First, wash your hands thoroughly.
  2. Place your index finger and thumb into your vagina. Pull the stem of the cup gently until you can reach the base.
  3. Pinch the base to release the air seal and pull down to remove the cup.
  4. Once it’s out, empty the cup into the sink or toilet. Wash cup thoroughly before re-inserting.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.

description:
How exactly do you use a menstrual cup?
Again, you're going to need to get super up close and personal with your vagina. Any cup you buy will come with lots of instructions about insertion and removal, the care and washing of your cup, and ways to troubleshoot common issues (you're definitely gonna want to read those).
“Menstrual cup usage has a learning curve, like anything else,” says Jyothi Parapurath, MD, ob-gyn practicing at Caremount Medical Group in New York. She explains that cups are folded and inserted into your vagina, where they seal themselves against the vaginal walls and collect your blood, ideally without any leakage.
So far, so good, right? But what about when it’s time to empty it? You’ll want to sit on the toilet for this part: Dr. Parapurath says to reach into your vagina, pull on the stem of the cup, grip its base, and keep pulling downward to break the suction keeping it in place. Once it slides out, dump the blood right into the toilet, rinse the cup off in the sink, and pop it back in.
